analysis.evidence: The animals go in two by two. אֶל־נֹחַ identifies whom they join, and אֶל־הַתֵּבָה identifies the ark as the place they enter.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine plural, with prefixed וַ־.

analysis.evidence: In וַיָּבֹאוּ אֶל נֹחַ, “they came to Noah,” the marked אֶל identifies Noah as the person the animals came to. The following אֶל הַתֵּבָה identifies the ark as their destination.
analysis.morphology: Preposition with no prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for נֹחַ linked to the root article nuach.
draft.definition: Noah, the son whom Lamech names in hope of relief from toil.
draft.evidence: Genesis 5:29 gives the name נֹחַ and explains it through the wordplay on יְנַחֲמֵנוּ, “he will comfort us.”

analysis.evidence: In וַיָּבֹאוּ אֶל־נֹחַ אֶל־הַתֵּבָה, “they came to Noah into the ark,” אֶל־נֹחַ identifies the person the creatures approached, and אֶל־הַתֵּבָה identifies the place they entered.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular proper noun with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: With וַיָּבֹאוּ (“they came”), אֶל נֹחַ identifies whom the animals joined, and the marked אֶל הַתֵּבָה identifies the place they entered.

draft.change: Add תֵּבָה under its own consonants, תבה, with senses for Noah’s ark and the papyrus basket in Exodus 2.

analysis.evidence: With וַיָּבֹאוּ, “they came,” the phrase אֶל נֹחַ identifies whom the creatures came to, and אֶל הַתֵּבָה identifies what they entered. שְׁנַיִם שְׁנַיִם describes their arrival in pairs.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הַ־ prefixed to a feminine singular absolute common noun, with doubling of the initial ת after the article.
analysis.sense: The vessel that carried Noah, his household, and the animals on the floodwaters.

analysis.evidence: The repetition שְׁנַיִם שְׁנַיִם modifies וַיָּבֹאוּ, describing how the living creatures came to Noah in the ark: two at a time.
analysis.morphology: Masculine dual absolute cardinal numeral, first occurrence in a distributive repetition.

analysis.evidence: The marked word is the second שְׁנַיִם in שְׁנַיִם שְׁנַיִם. The repetition describes how the creatures came to Noah in the ark, two at a time.
analysis.morphology: Masculine dual absolute cardinal numeral, repeated distributively.

analysis.evidence: מִכָּל הַבָּשָׂר means “from all flesh.” כָּל takes the collective noun הַבָּשָׂר as its complement, and מִן marks the group from which the creatures came two by two.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular construct noun with prefixed מִן, whose נ assimilates to כ.

analysis.evidence: מִכָּל הַבָּשָׂר means “from among all flesh.” The clause אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ רוּחַ חַיִּים identifies the creatures by the breath of life in them, and שְׁנַיִם שְׁנַיִם describes their coming to Noah in pairs.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הַ־ prefixed to a masculine singular absolute noun used collectively.
analysis.sense: all flesh: every living creature; mankind

analysis.evidence: אֲשֶׁר introduces a relative clause modifying כָּל הַבָּשָׂר. The suffix on בּוֹ refers back to הַבָּשָׂר, giving the phrase “all flesh in which there was the breath of life.”
analysis.morphology: Invariable relative particle without prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Add Genesis 7:15 to the evidence for the existing spatial sense be-in in article be.
draft.definition: בְּ marks the place or body within which something is present.
draft.evidence: Genesis 7:15 describes the creatures as flesh in which the breath of life is present. The suffixed preposition בּוֹ supplies ‘in it’ within the relative clause.

patch.value: "instrumental: b- 'with'"; "time, being in/at: b-"; "causal: b- 'on account of'"; compound prepositions "bd (b- + *-d- 'hand') and byd (b- + yd 'hand') 'in/from the hand(s)/power) of'; bqrb, btk 'in the midst of'".
"b-, b. /bi/ … variants: by; bm … prep. 'in' (place and direction, time), 'with,' 'for' (price) … 'from' … (H., Aram. b-, Arab. bi-)".

"b- passim; var b-m … var b-mw … IN, ON; BY MEANS OF; WITH; BY … (in invocations) [Cf Ar bi- passim; for use with enclitic -m(w), cf Ar bi-ma, Heb be-mō.]"; local, temporal, instrumental, "indicating accompaniment", "indicating exchange (rare): … 'in exchange for the well-being of their persons'".
"Ultimately Proto-Semitic *bV- ('with, in, at, among') … cognates with Ugaritic 𐎁 (b), Aramaic ב־, Classical Syriac ܒ-, Hebrew בְּ־ (bə-), Ge'ez ba- (bä)".

Scripture uses בְּ of the one God speaks by. Miriam and Aaron ask, "Has Yahweh spoken only by (בְּ) Moses? Has he not spoken by (בָּ) us also?" (Num 12:2); "the beginning of Yahweh's speaking by (בְּ) Hosea" (Hos 1:2); David says, "the Spirit of Yahweh spoke by me (בִּי), and his word was on my tongue" (2Sa 23:2), and Jesus reads a psalm as David speaking "by the Holy Spirit" (Mrk 12:36). Hebrews sets the Son in the same place: God, spoke to the fathers "in the prophets", "has in these last days spoken to us in a Son (ἐν υἱῷ), whom he appointed heir of all things" (Heb 1:1-2). In every case the speaker is God and the one he speaks by is the one he sent and appointed: the word the prophets and the Son spoke is God's own word.

To act "in" a name is to act with the authority of the one named. David goes against Goliath "in the name of Yahweh of hosts" (1Sa 17:45). Of the angel Yahweh sends before Israel he says, "obey his voice … for my name is in him (בְּקִרְבּוֹ)" (Exo 23:20-21): the angel is sent, and bears the name of the one who sends him. The psalm's "blessed is he who comes in the name of Yahweh" (Psa 118:26) is cried to Jesus as he enters Jerusalem (Mat 21:9), and that he says of himself, "I have come in my Father's name" (Jhn 5:43). So the one who comes in Yahweh's name is his sent representative, carrying his name and speaking with his authority, as the angel did.

Abraham "believed in (בְּ) Yahweh, and he counted it to him as righteousness" (Gen 15:6), and Habakkuk is told that "the righteous shall live by (בְּ) his faith" (Hab 2:4). The New Testament builds on both: "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness" (Rom 4:3), and "the righteous shall live by faith" (Rom 1:17 and Gal 3:11), set against being justified by law. The one preposition gives both sides: faith rests in Yahweh, and the righteous man's life comes by that faith.

Root investigation (2026-11-14). No root is shown; the entry is keyed by its own consonant ב, as le.json is keyed ל and min.json מנ. (1) The particle is one consonant with a short vowel in every language that has it (Hebrew bə-, Aramaic and Syriac b-, Ugaritic b /bi-/, Phoenician b-, Sabaic b-, Arabic bi-, Ge'ez ba-), and with suffixes is built on that letter alone (בּוֹ, בָּהֶם; Ugaritic bh, bhm; Arabic bihi). Akkadian has none (it uses ina). (2) The proposal from בַּיִת "house": Wiktionary's Arabic entry says bi- has a "likely interrelation with Proto-Semitic *bayt-", and its Hebrew entry traces *bV- to an Afroasiatic *bǔ "place" (Egyptian bw "place"). Against it: no form of the preposition in any language shows the y or the t of bayt (Ugaritic bt, Phoenician bt, Arabic bayt, Akkadian bītu all keep the t), the preposition's oldest attested sense range is as wide as its use with "house" is narrow, and no dictionary followed (Lane, Segert, Biella, Krahmalkov) derives it from "house". A parallel exists (Neo-Assyrian Akkadian bīt "where", a conjunction from bītu "house", Oracc), showing a word for house can become a word of place, but that is Akkadian and not the b- preposition. So the link is likeness of sound and sense only. בַּיִת has no entry yet (bayin.json leaves b.bo.ad, which carries the 2,320 tokens of בַּיִת, unclaimed); if a bayit entry is written, the proposal could be noted there too. The letter's name בֵּית is from the same word "house", but that says nothing of the preposition. Egyptian bw is not recorded as a cognate (the schema allows Egyptian only as a loan). (3) BDB keys: b.ab.aa named (1,386 tokens in the corpus: the 1,327 Hebrew free forms OSHB tags with the bare lemma b, 16 with וְ, 8 of בָּהֵן, 5 Aramaic, and others filed by spelling, among them 12 of בִּי "please" and 11 of בָּנוּ "they built" (lemma 1129)); b.ab.ab named (9 tokens, 8 of בְּמוֹ and Isa 25:10, Kethiv במו for בְּמֵי); xb.aa.aa named for the Aramaic (178 tokens, but only 30 are Aramaic; the rest are Hebrew surfaces it shares, 136, and 12 of בִּי "please", so its count is inflated as min.json's Aramaic key is). Left unclaimed: b.aa.aa (the letter's name, no tokens), b.ab.ac (BDB's cross-reference "see בֶּן־, see בֵּית" under בינ, no tokens), and the compounds BDB files elsewhere: בִּגְלַל (b.ae.ag, under גלל), בַּעֲבוּר, בְּטֶרֶם, בְּתוֹךְ, בְּקֶרֶב, בְּבִלְתִּי, entered here only as phrases. Token counts: OSHB tags 15,475 Hebrew words with a lemma segment b (all morphology R), of which 1,361 are free forms (morphology R with only a suffix, a pronoun or the conjunction besides; 1,327 of them with the bare lemma b) and 14,114 are prefixed and counted under their host words; Aramaic 225, 30 free. (4) Sources not consulted: Dillmann and Leslau for Ge'ez በ (Wiktionary only); Payne Smith for ܒ (SEDRA only); CAL for Aramaic; DULAT for Ugaritic; Moabite בּ in the Mesha inscription (no KAI source in sources.json). (5) The senses are illustrated, not exhaustive; the borders between "in a state", "with" and "by means of" are not sharp, and a verse can fit two of them (Exo 15:13; Psa 29:4). Act 3:25 in the TR quotes Gen 22:18 with the plain dative (τῷ σπέρματί σου), not ἐν, so it is not cited for ἐν. Doctrine: four points written evidence-first (blessed-in-the-seed, god-speaks-through-his-servants, in-the-name-of-yahweh, the-righteous-live-by-faith); the reviewer should check the framing of the last sentence of each.

analysis.evidence: In אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ רוּחַ חַיִּים, the suffix refers back to the masculine singular collective הַבָּשָׂר, ‘the flesh’. The relative clause means ‘in which is the breath of life’. בּוֹ locates the breath within the living creature.
analysis.morphology: Preposition בְּ with the third-person masculine singular pronominal suffix וֹ.

analysis.evidence: רוּחַ is in construct with חַיִּים, forming “breath of life.” The clause אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ רוּחַ חַיִּים describes the creatures entering the ark as having this breath in them.
analysis.morphology: Noun of common gender, singular construct, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ רוּחַ חַיִּים, “in which is the breath of life,” חַיִּים completes the construct phrase רוּחַ חַיִּים. The breath marks the creatures entering the ark as alive.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural absolute noun, with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: life as given by God's breath
